title: Linked List Cycle II
statement: Given the head of a singly linked list, return the node where a cycle begins, or null if there is no cycle. Use O(1) extra memory and do not modify the list.

nearMiss.why: A visited HashSet finds the entry, but it costs O(n) memory and the problem asks for O(1).
Reversing or rewiring links would modify the list, and it still wouldn't locate the entry node.
There is no far end to converge from: a singly linked list (possibly cyclic) is only walked forward.

trigger.why: A cycle in a 'next'-linked sequence with O(1) memory is Floyd's tortoise and hare: meet inside the cycle, then reset one pointer to find the entry.

ds.answer: Two ListNode references (slow, fast), then a third from head
ds.why: Pointers only; that is what makes it O(1) space.

invariant.answer: Inside the cycle, fast closes the gap to slow by one node per step, so they must meet; then head and the meeting point are equally far from the entry.
wrong: slow and fast are always the same distance apart.
fast reaches null exactly when a cycle exists.
The meeting point is always the cycle entry.
invariant.why: The distance algebra (2(a + b) = a + b + k·c ⇒ a = k·c − b) is why resetting one pointer to head works.

time.why: Each phase walks at most a constant number of laps.

wrong: A HashSet can't store ListNode objects.
Hashing would need the list sorted first.
A HashSet can detect a cycle but never its entry.

approach: slow += 1, fast += 2 until they meet (or fast hits null ⇒ no cycle). Then move a pointer from head and one from the meeting point one step at a time; where they meet is the entry.

title: Find the Duplicate Number
statement: An array of n + 1 integers holds values in the range 1..n, so at least one value repeats. Return the repeated value without modifying the array and using only O(1) extra space.

nearMiss.why: Swapping values into their home index finds it quickly, but it modifies the array, which is not allowed.
A HashSet finds it in O(n) time but needs O(n) extra space.
XOR cancellation only works when the duplicate appears exactly twice; here it may appear many times.

trigger.answer: without modifying the array and using only O(1) extra space
trigger.why: Values in 1..n can be read as 'next' links (i → nums[i]); a duplicate value means two links into one node: a cycle. No modification + O(1) space ⇒ Floyd.

ds.why: The array itself is the linked structure; two indices walk it.

invariant.answer: Following i → nums[i] from index 0 forms a path into a cycle, and the cycle's entry is the duplicated value.
wrong: The duplicate is always at index n.
nums[i] == i for every non-duplicate i.
The slow pointer only visits each index once in total.
invariant.why: Two indices hold the duplicate value, so two edges point at that node: the entry of the cycle.

time.why: Floyd's two phases are linear. (Binary search on the value range would be O(n log n).)

wrong: Cyclic sort only works on sorted arrays.
Cyclic sort needs values in 0..n−1, not 1..n.
Cyclic sort uses O(n) extra space.

approach: slow = nums[slow], fast = nums[nums[fast]] until equal. Then reset one to 0 and step both by one; where they meet is the duplicate.

title: Reverse Linked List
statement: Given the head of a singly linked list, reverse the list in place and return the new head.

nearMiss.why: Pushing nodes onto a stack and rebuilding works, but uses O(n) extra space; rewiring pointers is O(1).
Swapping values from both ends needs random access, which a singly linked list doesn't have.
Fast/slow finds positions (middle, cycle); reversal is about rewiring each link.

trigger.why: In-place reversal of links = the prev / curr / next three-pointer walk.

ds.answer: Three ListNode references: prev, curr, next
ds.why: Save next, point curr back to prev, advance.

invariant.answer: prev is the head of the already-reversed part; curr is the head of the untouched remainder.
wrong: prev always points to the original head.
The list is fully reversed after the first iteration.
invariant.why: Each step moves one node from the remainder to the front of the reversed part.

space.why: Three references (the recursive version uses O(n) stack).

wrong: A stack can't hold ListNode objects.
A stack would reverse the list twice.
A stack only works for lists with an even length.

approach: prev = null; while curr != null: next = curr.next; curr.next = prev; prev = curr; curr = next. Return prev.

title: Reverse Nodes in k-Group
statement: Reverse the nodes of a linked list k at a time and return the modified list. If fewer than k nodes remain at the end, leave them as they are. Use only O(1) extra memory.

nearMiss.why: A stack of k nodes reverses each group easily, but costs O(k) memory, and the problem asks for O(1).
Speed-difference pointers find middles and cycles; here you count k nodes and rewire them.
Swapping values from the ends of each group needs random access; a singly linked list only goes forward.

trigger.why: Reversing sub-lists in place = the reversal walk applied per group, with a dummy head to reconnect groups.

ds.answer: A dummy ListNode plus groupPrev / prev / curr / next references
ds.why: The dummy removes the head special case; groupPrev reconnects each reversed group.

invariant.answer: Everything before groupPrev.next is final; each group is reversed only after confirming k nodes exist.
wrong: Every group, including the last partial one, is reversed.
groupPrev always points to the original head.
The list length is always a multiple of k.
invariant.why: Checking k nodes ahead before rewiring keeps the tail intact.

time.why: Each node is visited a constant number of times (count ahead, then reverse).

wrong: A stack can't reverse linked-list nodes.
A stack would reverse the whole list instead of groups.
A stack only works when k is even.

approach: dummy → head. Repeatedly: find the kth node from groupPrev (stop if missing); reverse the group with the prev/curr walk; connect groupPrev to the new group head and the old group head to the next group; advance groupPrev.

title: Add Two Numbers
statement: Two non-empty linked lists store non-negative integers with their digits in reverse order (ones digit first). Add the two numbers and return the sum as a linked list in the same reverse-digit format.

nearMiss.why: Stacks are needed when digits are stored most-significant first (Add Two Numbers II); here they already come ones-first.
Converting the lists to int/long overflows for long numbers; add digit by digit with a carry.
Both lists advance one node per step; there is no speed difference involved.

wrong: return the sum as a linked list
trigger.why: Ones digit first means you can add left to right with a carry while building a new list behind a dummy head.

ds.answer: A dummy ListNode with a tail pointer, plus an int carry
ds.why: Build the result node by node; the carry is the only state.

invariant.answer: After each step, the result list holds the correct low digits of the sum so far, and carry is what flows into the next digit.
wrong: Both lists always have the same length.
The result list is built from the most significant digit.
invariant.why: Standard column addition, one column per node.

time.why: One pass over the longer list (plus a final carry).

space.answer: O(1) extra (the output list is not counted)
space.why: Only the carry and pointers besides the output.

wrong: A stack would make the sum overflow.
Stacks only work when both lists are the same length.

approach: dummy, tail, carry = 0. While either list or carry remains: sum = digits + carry; append sum % 10; carry = sum / 10; advance. Return dummy.next.

twists.change: Digits are stored most significant first, and you may not reverse the input lists.
twists.statement: Two non-empty linked lists store non-negative integers with the most significant digit first. Return their sum as a linked list in the same order, without reversing the input lists.
twists.ds: Two ArrayDeque<Integer> stacks of digits, building the result by prepending nodes

nearMiss.why: The usual trick is to reverse both lists first, which the problem now forbids.
Aligning the lists from the front doesn't let you carry from the back.
The stacks only reverse the digit order; nothing is kept sorted.

twists.why: You need the digits back-to-front without changing the lists ⇒ push them onto stacks, then pop and add with carry.
twists.approach: Push each list's digits. While stacks or carry: sum = pop1 + pop2 + carry; node = new ListNode(sum % 10); node.next = head; head = node.

title: Linked List Cycle
statement: Given the head of a singly linked list, return true if following next pointers ever revisits a node. Solve it with O(1) extra memory.

nearMiss.why: A HashSet of visited nodes detects the revisit, but it costs O(n) memory and the problem asks for O(1).
Reversing the list to see whether you return to head is clever but destroys the input and still needs care; two pointers just read it.
Converging pointers need a far end; a cyclic list has none.

trigger.why: Cycle in a next-linked structure + O(1) memory ⇒ Floyd's tortoise and hare.

ds.answer: Two ListNode references: slow (1 step) and fast (2 steps)

invariant.answer: Once both are inside a cycle, the gap between fast and slow shrinks by one node per step, so they must meet; if fast reaches null there is no cycle.
wrong: slow and fast are always one node apart.
fast always moves to the node slow just left.
They meet exactly at the cycle's first node.
invariant.why: Meeting point is somewhere in the cycle; finding the entry is Linked List Cycle II.

time.why: Fast catches slow within one lap of the cycle.

wrong: A HashSet can't store ListNode objects.
Hashing needs the values to be distinct.
A HashSet would miss cycles of length 1.

approach: slow = fast = head. While fast != null && fast.next != null: slow = slow.next; fast = fast.next.next; if slow == fast return true. Return false.

title: Happy Number
statement: Repeatedly replace a positive integer with the sum of the squares of its digits. It is happy if this reaches 1; otherwise the sequence loops endlessly without reaching 1. Decide whether n is happy.

nearMiss.why: There are no overlapping subproblems to tabulate: it is one deterministic sequence that either hits 1 or cycles.
The digit operation is decimal; bit tricks don't model it.
There is only one outgoing edge per number, so it is a single path, not a search: detecting the loop is all that's needed.

wrong: sum of the squares of its digits
trigger.why: A deterministic 'next' function that may cycle ⇒ Floyd's cycle detection (or a seen set).

ds.answer: Two ints: slow = next(n), fast = next(next(n))
wrong: int[] dp over all values up to n

invariant.answer: Every value maps to exactly one next value, so the sequence either reaches 1 (a fixed point) or enters a cycle, where fast must catch slow.
wrong: The sequence strictly decreases until it reaches 1.
slow and fast never share a value unless it is 1.
invariant.why: Values above 243 shrink fast, so the cycle (if any) is small.

time.why: Each step costs O(digits); after a few steps values are bounded by 243.

space.why: Two ints (a HashSet version is O(log n)).

wrong: DP would need n to be even.
DP is too slow for numbers over 100.

approach: slow = next(n), fast = next(next(n)); while fast != 1 && slow != fast, step them. Return fast == 1.

title: Merge Two Sorted Lists
statement: Given the heads of two sorted linked lists, splice their nodes together into one sorted list and return its head.

nearMiss.why: With exactly two lists, comparing the two heads is O(1); a heap only pays off for many lists.
There are two cursors, but the real work is relinking nodes behind a dummy head, which is the linked-list pattern.
Nothing is split around a pivot; two sorted runs are interleaved.

trigger.why: Building a list by relinking existing nodes ⇒ dummy head + tail pointer.

ds.answer: ListNode dummy, tail, and the two current heads
wrong: ArrayList<Integer> of all values, then sort
ds.why: A dummy head removes the 'first node' special case.

invariant.answer: dummy.next..tail is a sorted list of the smallest nodes taken so far, and every remaining node is ≥ tail.
wrong: tail always belongs to the first list.
Both lists are emptied at the same time.
The merged list is built from new nodes.
invariant.why: Take the smaller head each step; attach the leftover at the end.

space.why: Relinking only (the recursive version uses O(m + n) stack).

wrong: A heap can't store ListNode objects.
k-way merge requires lists of equal length.
A heap returns the largest node first.

approach: dummy, tail = dummy. While both non-null: attach the smaller head to tail and advance it. tail.next = whichever remains. Return dummy.next.

title: Remove Nth Node From End of List
statement: Given the head of a singly linked list, delete the n-th node counted from the end and return the head. Do it in one pass.

nearMiss.why: Two pointers do walk the list, but at the SAME speed with a fixed gap of n; there is no speed difference to exploit.
Pushing all nodes and popping n works, but takes O(n) space.
Converging from both ends isn't possible on a singly linked list.

trigger.why: Position from the end in one pass ⇒ lead pointer n + 1 ahead of a trailing pointer, both starting at a dummy head (so deleting the head is not special).

ds.answer: ListNode dummy plus two references: lead and trail
ds.why: The dummy makes removing the real head the same as any other node.

invariant.answer: lead is always n + 1 nodes ahead of trail, so when lead reaches null, trail.next is the node to delete.
wrong: lead moves two steps for every step of trail.
trail always points at the node to delete.
The gap shrinks by one each step.
Fast and slow pointers only work on cyclic lists.
Fast/slow would delete the middle node.
Fast/slow needs the list length first.

approach: dummy.next = head; lead = trail = dummy. Move lead n + 1 steps. Move both until lead == null. trail.next = trail.next.next. Return dummy.next.

title: Reorder List
statement: Rearrange a singly linked list L0 → L1 → … → Ln into L0 → Ln → L1 → Ln−1 → L2 → … by relinking nodes in place (values must not be modified).

nearMiss.why: Alternating first/last needs access from the back, which a singly linked list lacks until you reverse its second half.
Pushing all nodes onto a stack to pop from the end works, but uses O(n) space.
Fast/slow is only step 1 (find the middle); the core of the problem is reversing and interleaving links.

trigger.why: In-place relinking that needs the tail end ⇒ find middle, reverse second half, merge alternately.

ds.answer: ListNode references: slow/fast to find the middle, prev/curr/next to reverse, two cursors to merge
wrong: ArrayDeque<ListNode> as a deque of all nodes

invariant.answer: After cutting at the middle and reversing the second half, both halves are in the order needed, and the merge takes one node from each in turn.
wrong: The second half is always longer than the first.
The middle node moves to the end.
invariant.why: The first half has the same length as the second, or one more.

wrong: Two pointers can't be used with ListNode objects.
Two pointers would sort the list.
Two pointers needs the list to be sorted.

approach: Find the middle with slow/fast; cut. Reverse the second half. Merge: a.next = b, b.next = a's old next, advance both.
